Q001215:
Why this is correct:
Cross-Region actions need an artifact store per Region. CodePipeline copies artifacts to the Region's bucket, and each Region's KMS key policy must allow the roles that read them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-S3 because KMS can't cross Regions: per-Region keys are the answer.
• GetObject only: SSE-KMS artifacts also need kms:Decrypt.
• CRR instead: CodePipeline manages cross-Region artifacts itself.

Key takeaway: cross-Region pipelines → artifact store (bucket + key) per Region.
Q001216:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager with RDS rotation holds the credentials, and the buildspec references it as a secrets-manager environment variable, so nothing is stored in code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameter Store rotated by a Lambda: custom rotation.
• Plaintext in buildspec: exposed in the repo.
• S3 file: weak secret handling.

Key takeaway: build-time DB secrets → Secrets Manager reference.
Q001217:
Why this is correct:
A CodeConnections (CodeStar Connections) GitHub source action uses a GitHub app installation and webhooks, starting the pipeline on pushes without stored tokens.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Polling: delayed and not the recommended approach.
• Scheduled starts: not event-driven.
• GitHub v1 with a PAT: legacy and stores a token.

Key takeaway: GitHub source → CodeConnections.
Q001218:
Why this is correct:
Static values fit Parameter Store SecureString (low cost), while credentials needing rotation belong in Secrets Manager.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All in advanced Parameter Store with custom rotation: reinvents Secrets Manager.
• All in Secrets Manager: more cost for static values.
• Encrypted env vars per project: duplicated and hard to update.

Key takeaway: match the store to the need for rotation.
Q001220:
Why this is correct:
Each VPC-connected CodeBuild build uses an ENI, and a /28 subnet has only 11 usable IPs, so more concurrent builds fail to launch.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RDS connection limit: would cause DB errors, not launch failures.
• No VPC support for concurrency: incorrect.
• SG blocking: would fail single builds too.

Key takeaway: VPC builds consume subnet IPs.
Q001222:
Why this is correct:
Migrating means translating Jenkins stages into CodePipeline stages and buildspec commands for CodeBuild.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeStar conversion: no such conversion.
• Jenkins inside CodeBuild: not managed CI/CD.
• Lambda for every stage: poor fit.

Key takeaway: rebuild the pipeline natively.
Q001223:
Why this is correct:
Effective permissions are the intersection of the role's policies and its permissions boundary. If the boundary omits cloudformation:CreateStack, the build can't create stacks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• buildspec action lists: not how IAM works.
• Boundaries only for users: they apply to roles too.
• CodeBuild ignores boundaries: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: boundaries cap permissions.
Q001224:
Why this is correct:
A versioned CloudFormation or CDK template instantiated per team keeps every pipeline identical and updatable centrally.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Copying JSON: drift.
• Config rules after creation: detection only.
• Console runbook: manual.

Key takeaway: pipelines as code.
Q001226:
Why this is correct:
Polling adds start latency and more API calls compared with event-based triggers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No tradeoff: there is one.
• More secure: not inherently.
• Polling eliminates cost: not true.

Key takeaway: prefer event-driven triggers.
Q001228:
Why this is correct:
A CodeBuild webhook on pull request events runs builds, and a required status check in GitHub blocks merging failing PRs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeDeploy hook: deployment, not PR checks.
• Manual builds: unreliable.
• Full pipeline polling: slow and heavy.

Key takeaway: PR validation → webhook + required status check.
Q001229:
Why this is correct:
A SAST step in the build that exits non-zero on high-severity findings fails the build automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scan after production: too late.
• Manual review later: not a gate.
• Macie: finds sensitive data, not code vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: security gates must fail the build.
Q001230:
Why this is correct:
A staging load-test stage that measures p99 latency and fails the pipeline when the SLA is breached prevents slow releases from reaching production.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ValidateService in production: too late and not load testing.
• Local manual tests: inconsistent.
• Monitor production: users are affected.

Key takeaway: performance gates before production.
Q001231:
Why this is correct:
ValidateService runs after the application starts, and a non-zero exit fails that instance's deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't customize: hooks can.
• ApplicationStop: before install.
• BeforeInstall: before new code exists.

Key takeaway: health validation → ValidateService.
Q001232:
Why this is correct:
A Lambda invoke action runs custom logic and reports the result with PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS async: no result reported to the pipeline.
• Manual approval: not automated.
• Impossible: Lambda actions exist.

Key takeaway: custom pipeline steps → Lambda invoke action.
Q001233:
Why this is correct:
A custom CodeBuild image with the browser and WebDriver installed runs Selenium tests headlessly against staging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't run Selenium: it can.
• Cached browsers on the default image: unreliable.
• Local runs with screenshots: not automated.

Key takeaway: special tooling → custom build image.
Q001234:
Why this is correct:
An isolated, ephemeral database per execution prevents concurrent runs from colliding on shared test data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger instance: doesn't isolate data.
• Drop integration tests: loses coverage.
• Serialize all runs: slows delivery.

Key takeaway: isolate test data per run.
Q001236:
Why this is correct:
Running unit tests in the build phase fails fast before packaging. A separate test stage isolates concerns but adds pipeline time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Impossible before packaging: it's common.
• Only after deployment: unit tests don't need a live environment.
• No difference: they differ.

Key takeaway: test placement trades speed for separation.
Q001237:
Why this is correct:
The custom action should submit the scan, then report success or failure only when the real verdict is available (for example, via continuation tokens or callbacks).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Report success immediately: unsafe.
• Manual dashboard check: not automated.
• CodeBuild sleep loop: wastes build minutes.

Key takeaway: async external checks → report the real result.
Q001239:
Why this is correct:
Associating the repository with CodeGuru Reviewer adds PR recommendations, and a build check can fail on open critical findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual copy: not automated.
• GitHub only: CodeCommit is supported.
• CodeGuru Profiler: runtime performance.

Key takeaway: PR code review automation → CodeGuru Reviewer.
Q001240:
Why this is correct:
Sequential stages per environment, each running its required test depth, promote only builds that pass each gate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All tests at start: environments differ.
• Parallel deploy: skips gating.
• One environment: no isolation.

Key takeaway: progressive promotion with gates.
Q001241:
Why this is correct:
A CodeArtifact repository with an internal upstream and an external connection to public registries serves approved internal packages and proxies public ones.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't connect public: it can.
• S3 as registry: loses package manager features.
• Separate unconnected repositories: confusing for developers.

Key takeaway: internal + public packages → upstreams and external connections.
Q001242:
Why this is correct:
ECR enhanced scanning with Inspector continuously rescans images when new CVEs are published.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Basic scanning: only at push.
• Re-pushing daily: hacky.
• Macie: not vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: continuous image scanning → enhanced scanning.
Q001244:
Why this is correct:
An S3 lifecycle policy transitions and expires old artifacts automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EFS: more expensive.
• Delete and recreate the bucket: loses recent artifacts.
• Disabling artifacts: breaks pipelines.

Key takeaway: artifact growth → lifecycle rules.
Q001246:
Why this is correct:
Container images in ECR support up to 10 GB, fitting large ML libraries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Split into many functions: complexity.
• Support increase: the zip limit isn't raised this way.
• Batch only: Lambda can run ML libraries via images.

Key takeaway: large Lambda dependencies → container image.
Q001247:
Why this is correct:
CodeArtifact domain and repository resource policies grant other accounts the read actions they need.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AdministratorAccess: over-privileged.
• Copies to S3: duplication.
• Can't share: it can.

Key takeaway: cross-account package access → resource policies.
Q001248:
Why this is correct:
ECR private registry replication copies images to other Regions automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 CRR: not for ECR.
• ECR can't replicate: it can.
• Scripts: manual.

Key takeaway: multi-Region images → ECR replication.
Q001249:
Why this is correct:
One CodeBuild project can run commands that build and push an image to ECR and package a Lambda zip, with secondary artifacts if needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only one output: projects can produce several.
• Split repos: unnecessary.
• CodeDeploy builds images: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: one build can produce multiple artifacts.
Q001250:
Why this is correct:
Image Builder with STIG hardening and test components builds and validates compliant AMIs on a schedule.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config after launch: detection, not hardened images.
• One manual AMI forever: goes stale.
• Inspector modifies AMIs: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: compliant golden AMIs → Image Builder with STIG components.
Q001251:
Why this is correct:
If a new upstream is searched first but isn't itself connected to the public registry, resolution can fail. Ensure the chain links to the repository with the external connection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hardcoded allowlist: not true.
• npm unsupported: it is supported.
• One upstream only: repositories can have several.

Key takeaway: check upstream order and connectivity.
Q001252:
Why this is correct:
An ECR lifecycle policy rule expires untagged images automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual deletion: toil.
• Enhanced scanning: doesn't delete.
• Tag immutability: prevents overwrites; doesn't clean up.

Key takeaway: image cleanup → lifecycle policies.
Q001253:
Why this is correct:
With a customer managed key, the key policy must allow Account B, and the repository policy must allow B to pull.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Admin on the key: over-privileged.
• Copy the key: keys can't be copied.
• Disable encryption: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: cross-account encrypted ECR → key policy + repository policy.
Q001255:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS supports canary and linear traffic shifting with alarm-based rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rolling updates shift percentages: they don't.
• Identical: they differ.
• Rolling with alarm rollback shifting traffic: not the same capability.

Key takeaway: traffic shifting for ECS → CodeDeploy blue/green.
Q001256:
Why this is correct:
LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes shifts 10% first, waits 10 minutes, then shifts the rest.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AllAtOnce: no gradual shift.
• Linear: equal steps each interval.
• Lambda full cutover only: false.

Key takeaway: 10% then all after waiting → canary.
Q001257:
Why this is correct:
Argo Rollouts or Flagger provide blue/green and canary strategies with metric-based promotion for Kubernetes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rolling only: not true with these tools.
• CodeDeploy ECS for EKS: not supported.
• Manual replica edits: error-prone.

Key takeaway: progressive delivery on EKS → Argo Rollouts / Flagger.
Q001259:
Why this is correct:
Blue/green creates new instances with fresh volumes, so local session data is lost. Externalize session state first.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic EBS migration: doesn't happen.
• Can't use EBS: it can for stateless apps.
• In-place loses data: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: externalize state before immutable deployments.
Q001260:
Why this is correct:
Deploy the new version to a separate bucket (or prefix), validate it, then switch the CloudFront origin, keeping the old one for rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeDeploy hook: not for S3.
• Doesn't apply: it does.
• Overwrite and invalidate: no clean rollback.

Key takeaway: static blue/green → switch origins.
Q001261:
Why this is correct:
EFS is a shared file system, so the green fleet can mount the same file system. Verify mount configuration and NFS security group rules for new instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EFS incompatible with ASGs: it isn't.
• Separate EFS per fleet: duplicates data.
• Manual copies: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: shared state lives outside instances.
Q001262:
Why this is correct:
AllAtOnce is fastest but removes all capacity during deployment. OneAtATime is safest but slowest.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Configs only for Lambda/ECS: EC2 supports them.
• OneAtATime is concurrent: it isn't.
• AllAtOnce safest: it isn't.

Key takeaway: deployment speed vs. capacity risk.
Q001263:
Why this is correct:
A failed hook marks the deployment Failed. Without automatic rollback configured, instances are left with mixed versions until redeployed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Failure ignored: not true.
• Terminates instances: not true.
• Rollback by default: must be enabled.

Key takeaway: configure automatic rollback.
Q001264:
Why this is correct:
During traffic shifting, both versions use the same database. Expand-and-contract schema changes keep the schema compatible with both.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recreate the DB: data loss.
• Lambda-only issue: applies to all.
• Migrated copy: blue/green doesn't copy databases.

Key takeaway: shared databases need backward-compatible changes.
Q001265:
Why this is correct:
Canary shifts a portion once, then the rest after a wait. Linear shifts equal increments at regular intervals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same behavior: different.
• Manual approval between steps: not required.
• Always 50/50: not true.

Key takeaway: canary = two steps; linear = many equal steps.
Q001266:
Why this is correct:
New tasks marked unhealthy during startup need a longer health check grace period and suitable target group health settings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fewer tasks: doesn't fix health.
• Disable health checks: unsafe.
• Rolling updates: still need health.

Key takeaway: slow starts → grace period and health tuning.
Q001268:
Why this is correct:
The CDK lets you define reusable constructs in code, reducing repetition, and cdk synth shows the generated templates for review.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nested stacks only: still JSON repetition.
• Macros only: not the only way to add logic.
• OpsWorks: configuration management.

Key takeaway: repetitive templates → CDK constructs.
Q001270:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation modules in the registry package a governed, versioned building block that templates can reuse.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hardcoded nested stack URL: weak versioning.
• StackSets: deployment, not a reusable building block.
• Service Catalog product: for launching products, not composing within templates.

Key takeaway: reusable template components → modules.
Q001271:
Why this is correct:
AppConfig deploys configuration or feature flags gradually, monitors alarms, and rolls back automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Secrets Manager rotation: secrets.
• Parameter Store: no gradual rollout.
• Change sets: infrastructure.

Key takeaway: gradual config rollout → AppConfig.
Q001272:
Why this is correct:
Credentials go in Secrets Manager with rotation, and other configuration in Parameter Store.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom rotation in Parameter Store: reinvents Secrets Manager.
• Only Secrets Manager supported: both have dynamic references.
• Credentials in Parameter Store: no managed rotation.

Key takeaway: secrets vs. config: different stores.
Q001274:
Why this is correct:
Nested stacks are managed as part of one parent stack's lifecycle. Exports and imports connect independently managed stacks (and exported values can't change while imported).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Exports change freely: they can't while imported.
• Resource types swapped: incorrect.
• Identical: they differ.

Key takeaway: same lifecycle → nested; independent → exports.
Q001275:
Why this is correct:
A low failure tolerance and concurrency settings caused StackSets to stop early. Fix the failing accounts' issues and adjust FailureToleranceCount and MaxConcurrentCount.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No tolerance settings: they exist.
• Halts on any failure: configurable.
• Same OU required: not true.

Key takeaway: tune StackSets operation preferences.
Q001276:
Why this is correct:
A CDK Aspect visits every construct during synthesis and can raise an error for unencrypted buckets, enforcing policy before deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• StackSet after deployment: too late.
• Config rule after creation: detective.
• Context value: doesn't enforce.

Key takeaway: policy checks at synth → Aspects.
Q001277:
Why this is correct:
A Lambda custom resource must send its result to the pre-signed S3 response URL. Returning directly leaves CloudFormation waiting until timeout.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Must be a macro: no.
• Missing invoke permission: CloudFormation invokes via the service token.
• No external HTTP: allowed.

Key takeaway: custom resources must signal the response URL.
Q001279:
Why this is correct:
A guardrail that blocks disabling Config is preventive (SCP). One that reports buckets without logging is detective (Config rule).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both preventive: one detects.
• Both detective: one blocks.
• Reversed: incorrect.

Key takeaway: block = SCP; detect = Config.
Q001280:
Why this is correct:
The role's trust policy requires sts:ExternalId, and the vendor's AssumeRole call must pass the matching ExternalId; a missing or wrong value denies it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identity Center required: not for this.
• Same organization: not required.
• Can't include ExternalId: it's the standard for third parties.

Key takeaway: third-party roles → ExternalId.
Q001281:
Why this is correct:
SCPs at every level of the hierarchy apply together. An explicit Deny at an ancestor can't be overridden below.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lower overrides higher: false.
• Allow overrides Deny: false.
• Identity deny required: not needed.

Key takeaway: SCPs accumulate down the tree.
Q001282:
Why this is correct:
A GuardDuty delegated administrator manages configuration and findings for all accounts, and auto-enable covers new accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Management account only: no coverage.
• Manual invitations: toil.
• Config enabling GuardDuty: not how it works.

Key takeaway: org-wide GuardDuty → delegated admin + auto-enable.
Q001283:
Why this is correct:
Account Factory exposed as a Service Catalog product, shared only with approved developers, provides governed self-service accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Direct CreateAccount access: no guardrails.
• Conformance packs creating accounts: not possible.
• Tickets: not self-service.

Key takeaway: self-service accounts → Account Factory.
Q001284:
Why this is correct:
An SCP at the root denying actions when aws:PrincipalOrgID isn't the organization's ID (for example, with resource conditions) prevents access by outside principals across all accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Block Public Access: doesn't restrict to the organization.
• Bucket policy only: protects one bucket, not all.
• Config deletion: after the fact.

Key takeaway: org-only access → aws:PrincipalOrgID conditions.
Q001285:
Why this is correct:
Control Tower drift is resolved by re-registering the OU, repairing, or updating the landing zone so resources match the baseline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Blocking all CloudTrail calls: breaks things.
• Manual revert clears drift automatically: not always.
• Remove and re-register: disruptive.

Key takeaway: fix drift through Control Tower.
Q001286:
Why this is correct:
Tag policies define allowed CostCenter values and report noncompliance, but on their own they don't block creation of untagged resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCP only way: tag policies and SCPs complement.
• Budgets enforce tags: they don't.
• Organizations has no tagging enforcement: tag policies exist.

Key takeaway: tag policies standardize; SCPs block.
Q001287:
Why this is correct:
Raise the role's MaxSessionDuration (up to 12 hours) and request a longer DurationSeconds in AssumeRole.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ExternalId: doesn't extend sessions.
• 15-minute limit: false.
• GetFederationToken never expires: false.

Key takeaway: long jobs → longer role sessions.
Q001288:
Why this is correct:
A Standard workflow can wait for approval with a task token (hours), branch with Choice, and remediate or notify.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Express: 5-minute limit.
• Lambda sleeping: 15-minute limit.
• Lambda retries: not approval.

Key takeaway: long, auditable remediation → Standard workflow + task token.
Q001289:
Why this is correct:
A Config remediation configuration running an SSM Automation document can fix noncompliant buckets automatically within minutes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Paging on-call: manual.
• Aggregators: view only.
• Trusted Advisor: doesn't remediate Config rules.

Key takeaway: auto-fix Config findings → remediation actions.
Q001290:
Why this is correct:
A custom Lambda-backed Config rule can implement conditional logic and report results with PutEvaluations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFormation Hook: pre-provisioning only.
• required-tags: can't express conditional logic.
• Trusted Advisor custom checks: not a feature.

Key takeaway: custom compliance logic → custom Config rule.
Q001292:
Why this is correct:
Express workflows suit high-volume, short event processing. Standard workflows suit long-running, auditable remediation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Express for both: Express has a 5-minute limit.
• Reversed: incorrect.
• Standard for both: costly for high volume.

Key takeaway: high-volume short → Express; long auditable → Standard.
Q001293:
Why this is correct:
SDK retries with exponential backoff and jitter handle throttling, and reducing concurrency lowers the request rate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CLI isn't throttled: it is.
• Lambda concurrency: not the source.
• Stop and log: loses automation.

Key takeaway: throttling → backoff + less concurrency.
Q001294:
Why this is correct:
SSM Inventory collects installed software versions, and a custom Config rule can evaluate whether the approved version is present.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector reachability: not software versions.
• CloudTrail: API calls.
• Trusted Advisor: no software inventory.

Key takeaway: software compliance → Inventory + Config.
Q001295:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on the CloudTrail event starts a Step Functions workflow that notifies Slack and remediates within seconds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hourly cron scan: slow.
• Config rule sending Slack and remediating: slower and mixes concerns.
• 24-hour periodic rule: too slow.

Key takeaway: react to API calls in near real time → EventBridge + CloudTrail.
Q001296:
Why this is correct:
State Manager associations support rate controls: MaxConcurrency limits how many targets run at once, and MaxErrors stops after a threshold.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Maintenance Windows only: associations have controls.
• CloudWatch alarm pause: not a feature here.
• MaxErrors only: MaxConcurrency exists too.

Key takeaway: fleet-safe rollout → rate controls.
Q001297:
Why this is correct:
Systems Manager integrates natively and needs no Chef or Puppet server. Plan to move configuration from cookbooks to SSM documents or State Manager.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OpsWorks recommended: it's end of life.
• SSM can't manage on-prem: it can.
• Cookbooks run unmodified: not directly.

Key takeaway: migrate off OpsWorks to Systems Manager.
Q001298:
Why this is correct:
A Retry with backoff on the Task handles transient throttling, and a Catch routes persistent failures to a cleanup state.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parallel state: doesn't add retries.
• Wait state: can't prevent throttling.
• Default retries: Task states don't retry by default.

Key takeaway: Retry + Catch on tasks.
Q001299:
Why this is correct:
Automation supports multi-account, multi-Region executions using an execution role in each target account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Run Command only: Automation supports it.
• Config aggregators run runbooks: they don't.
• Manual copies: toil.

Key takeaway: run runbooks across accounts → multi-account Automation.
Q001300:
Why this is correct:
RDS Multi-AZ failover updates the endpoint's DNS record to the new primary. Apps that cache the resolved IP longer than the short TTL keep connecting to the old host; fix DNS caching (for example, the JVM TTL).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda to update DNS: RDS already does this.
• Only Aurora: RDS Multi-AZ also fails over DNS.
• Security groups: they apply to both instances.

Key takeaway: Multi-AZ failover = same name, new IP.
Q001301:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB Global Tables provide multi-Region, multi-writer replication with low-latency local reads and writes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Aurora Global: one writer Region.
• ElastiCache cross-Region: one primary for writes.
• RDS replicas: read-only.

Key takeaway: multi-Region writes → Global Tables.
Q001302:
Why this is correct:
A CloudFront origin group fails over to the replicated bucket automatically on specified error status codes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate distributions with DNS: slower and more complex.
• Lambda@Edge redirects: custom and brittle.
• Transfer Acceleration: uploads.

Key takeaway: origin failover → origin groups.
Q001305:
Why this is correct:
Global Tables resolve concurrent writes to the same item with last-writer-wins. Use conditional writes, route writes for an item to one Region, or design to avoid multi-Region conflicts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Strict global order: not guaranteed.
• Streams: don't enforce consistency.
• Transactions: apply within a Region, not across replicas.

Key takeaway: multi-active means conflict handling is your job.
Q001306:
Why this is correct:
Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing controls switch traffic across interdependent records together, and safety rules prevent unsafe states such as both Regions off.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Conformance packs: compliance.
• Separate SSM documents: no coordinated safety.
• Longer health check intervals: slower detection.

Key takeaway: coordinated, safe Regional failover → ARC routing controls.
Q001307:
Why this is correct:
A Network Load Balancer handles long-lived TCP connections at Layer 4 with low latency and static IPs. (ALB also supports gRPC, but the answer here is based on Layer 4 needs.)

Why the other options are wrong:
• Classic LB: legacy.
• GWLB: for appliances.
• ALB: supports gRPC over HTTP/2, but not the chosen Layer 4 requirements.

Key takeaway: long-lived Layer 4 connections → NLB.
Q001308:
Why this is correct:
Multi-AZ DB clusters have two readable standbys and a reader endpoint. Multi-AZ DB instances have one non-readable standby.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both readable: instance standby isn't.
• Instances fail over faster: clusters are typically faster.
• Aurora only: clusters exist for RDS MySQL and PostgreSQL.

Key takeaway: readable standbys → Multi-AZ DB cluster.
Q001309:
Why this is correct:
In a serial chain, availability multiplies (0.9995 × 0.9999 × ...), so the weakest single-AZ database dominates. Enabling Multi-AZ on RDS raises the overall availability most.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Additive: availability multiplies.
• Only the least reliable matters: all multiply.
• Serverless excluded: still in the path.

Key takeaway: serial dependencies multiply risk.
Q001310:
Why this is correct:
Target tracking on ALBRequestCountPerTarget scales tasks in proportion to incoming requests.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled only: misses spikes.
• Manual: slow.
• Single large CPU step: coarse.

Key takeaway: request-driven services → scale on requests per target.
Q001311:
Why this is correct:
Karpenter provisions right-sized nodes directly from pending pod requirements, across diverse instance types (including Spot), scaling faster than Cluster Autoscaler's node-group model.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cluster Autoscaler Spot only: Karpenter supports Spot.
• Runs only outside EKS: false.
• Identical: they differ.

Key takeaway: flexible, fast EKS node provisioning → Karpenter.
Q001312:
Why this is correct:
HTTP 429 from API Gateway means rate or burst throttling limits were exceeded (account, stage, method, or usage plan).

Why the other options are wrong:
• DLQ full: unrelated.
• Usage plan mandatory: not required.
• Reserved concurrency too high: would not cause 429 from API Gateway.

Key takeaway: 429 = throttling.
Q001313:
Why this is correct:
Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized, avoiding cold starts. Reserved concurrency only guarantees and caps concurrency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reserved pre-initializes: it doesn't.
• Memory equals concurrency: false.
• SnapStart for every runtime: limited runtimes, and it doesn't replace concurrency settings.

Key takeaway: cold starts → provisioned concurrency (or SnapStart).
Q001314:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway stage caching reduces backend calls at the Region, while CloudFront caches at edge locations near users. They can be combined.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Mutually exclusive: they can coexist.
• CloudFront can't cache API Gateway: it can.
• Only CloudFront has TTL: stage caches have TTLs.

Key takeaway: edge caching and API caching complement each other.
Q001315:
Why this is correct:
Predictive scaling forecasts load from history and schedules capacity ahead of expected demand.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replaces min/max: they still apply.
• Spot only: not a restriction.
• Pre-launches every type: no.

Key takeaway: recurring patterns → predictive scaling.
Q001316:
Why this is correct:
Storing session state in ElastiCache or DynamoDB means scale-in doesn't lose sessions, regardless of stickiness.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Never terminate sticky instances: blocks scaling.
• 7-day cookies: still lost on termination.
• Disable Auto Scaling: loses elasticity.

Key takeaway: externalize session state.
Q001317:
Why this is correct:
Target tracking adjusts capacity to keep a metric at a target, with less tuning than step scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Step always faster: not necessarily.
• No custom metrics: target tracking supports them.
• Scheduled only: misses variation.

Key takeaway: hold a metric steady → target tracking.
Q001318:
Why this is correct:
Warm pools keep pre-initialized instances ready (stopped or running), so scale-out skips lengthy setup.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer cooldown: slows scaling.
• Termination hooks: shutdown, not startup.
• Larger instances: don't remove setup time.

Key takeaway: slow instance initialization → warm pools.
Q001319:
Why this is correct:
ElastiCache for Redis (or Valkey) supports rich data structures, replication, and Multi-AZ failover, which fits dashboard caching needing resilience.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Memcached throughput: no replication or failover.
• Either engine: Memcached lacks failover.
• Memcached: same issue.

Key takeaway: cache with HA and data structures → Redis/Valkey.
Q001320:
Why this is correct:
Latency spikes at deployments come from cold starts. Provisioned concurrency with Application Auto Scaling (target tracking), or SnapStart where supported, keeps environments warm.

Why the other options are wrong:
• arm64 to x86: doesn't eliminate cold starts.
• Reserved concurrency at the limit: no warmth.
• Maximum timeout: unrelated.

Key takeaway: deployment cold starts → provisioned concurrency.
Q001321:
Why this is correct:
Reboot with failover triggers a real Multi-AZ failover so the team can measure behavior and recovery time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Blocking SGs: not a failover test.
• Manual DNS edits: not how RDS works.
• Deleting the standby: not possible or safe.

Key takeaway: test Multi-AZ failover → reboot with failover.
Q001322:
Why this is correct:
Backup and restore costs least but recovers slowest. Pilot light keeps core data replicated and running, costing more but recovering faster.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Not a strategy: it is.
• Pilot light costs more than active-active: false.
• Identical RTO: they differ.

Key takeaway: DR cost rises as recovery time falls.
Q001323:
Why this is correct:
Route 53 ARC readiness checks continuously verify that the standby's resources and quotas match the primary.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Quarterly scripts: infrequent.
• Billing alarms: unrelated.
• Trusted Advisor cost checks: unrelated.

Key takeaway: continuous DR readiness → ARC readiness checks.
Q001324:
Why this is correct:
Incident Manager response plans standardize detection-to-response: engagement, runbooks, and chat channels when an alarm fires.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: best practices.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.
• Config drift: configuration.

Key takeaway: standard incident response → Incident Manager.
Q001325:
Why this is correct:
If tasks pass shallow health checks while deadlocked, publish a true-health custom metric (or deep health endpoint) and alarm on it to trigger replacement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ECS detects deadlocks automatically: only if health checks test it.
• Longer interval: slower detection.
• Disable health checks: unsafe.

Key takeaway: health checks must reflect real functionality.
Q001326:
Why this is correct:
AWS Fault Injection Service runs controlled experiments with stop conditions to validate failover procedures safely.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector terminating instances: not its purpose.
• CloudTrail replay: doesn't simulate failures.
• Config terminating resources: not fault injection.

Key takeaway: validate resilience → FIS experiments.
Q001328:
Why this is correct:
A metric filter counting ERROR entries publishes a metric, and an alarm triggers when it exceeds a threshold.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled queries: delayed.
• S3 export notifications: slow.
• IncomingBytes anomaly: not error-specific.

Key takeaway: alarms on log patterns → metric filters.
Q001329:
Why this is correct:
Subscription filters stream logs from many groups to Kinesis, which feeds OpenSearch for near-real-time search and dashboards, with raw copies in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights access: not a central search platform.
• Metric streams: metrics, not logs.
• Nightly exports: not near real time.

Key takeaway: central log search → subscriptions to OpenSearch.
Q001330:
Why this is correct:
The KMS key policy must allow the CloudWatch Logs service principal for the Region to use the key; otherwise writes fail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No customer keys: they're supported.
• Caller needs Decrypt: the service uses the key.
• Never expire needed: unrelated.

Key takeaway: encrypted log groups need key policy permissions.
Q001331:
Why this is correct:
Keep a short retention in CloudWatch Logs, export (or subscribe) logs to S3, and lifecycle them to Glacier Deep Archive for the 7-year period.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recreate groups: loses data.
• Intelligent-Tiering on log groups: not available.
• Never expire: expensive.

Key takeaway: long retention → S3 archive, not CloudWatch.
Q001332:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch metric streams continuously send metrics through Firehose to third-party destinations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled GetMetricData: API cost and gaps.
• Log subscriptions: logs, not metrics.
• Public dashboards: not data export.

Key takeaway: continuous metric export → metric streams.
Q001333:
Why this is correct:
One metric name with a TenantId dimension supports per-tenant views, and publishing an additional dimensionless aggregate (or using metric math/Metrics Insights) gives totals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Publish twice: works but the option describes it inefficiently.
• Logs only: no metrics.
• Metric per tenant: explodes metric names.

Key takeaway: use dimensions for per-entity metrics.
Q001334:
Why this is correct:
Selecting fields, sorting by durationMs descending, and limiting to 10 returns the slowest requests.

Why the other options are wrong:
• avg: one number.
• parse without sort: no ordering.
• count: not the slowest.

Key takeaway: top-N → sort desc + limit.
Q001335:
Why this is correct:
The embedded metric format writes metrics inside structured log lines, which CloudWatch extracts asynchronously, with no extra API calls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• PutMetricData per order: latency and throttling.
• Container Insights: containers.
• X-Ray annotations: tracing.

Key takeaway: Lambda custom metrics → EMF.
Q001336:
Why this is correct:
Subscription filters in each account send logs to a Kinesis stream (or Firehose) destination in the security account, centralizing them continuously.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Assume roles to poll: inefficient.
• Consolidated billing: unrelated.
• Nightly S3 exports and email: slow.

Key takeaway: cross-account log centralization → subscription destinations.
Q001337:
Why this is correct:
The instance role must allow cloudwatch:PutMetricData (and ssm:GetParameter if the agent config is in Parameter Store).

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail: unrelated.
• Auto Scaling: unrelated.
• Public IP: not needed with endpoints or NAT.

Key takeaway: agent metrics missing → check role permissions.
Q001339:
Why this is correct:
High-resolution metrics enable alarms with 10-second periods but cost more than standard resolution.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Standard supports 10-second alarms: no.
• High resolution cheaper: no.
• Only dashboards: affects alarms too.

Key takeaway: sub-minute alarms need high resolution.
Q001340:
Why this is correct:
Anomaly detection alarms learn daily and weekly patterns and alert when values fall outside the expected band.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fixed-filter queries: no seasonality.
• Config rules: not metric evaluation.
• Static peak threshold: misses anomalies.

Key takeaway: seasonal metrics → anomaly detection.
Q001341:
Why this is correct:
Athena can query CloudTrail logs in S3 with SQL by defining a table (or using partition projection) over the log location.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights re-upload: unnecessary.
• Config: resource configuration.
• RDS import: heavy.

Key takeaway: SQL over CloudTrail in S3 → Athena.
Q001342:
Why this is correct:
QuickSight builds polished, interactive dashboards, supports embedding, and offers row-level security for business audiences.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudWatch dashboards: operational, not BI.
• Config aggregator dashboards: compliance.
• Inspector reports: vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: business dashboards → QuickSight.
Q001343:
Why this is correct:
Custom X-Ray sampling rules lower sampling for noisy, low-value routes and keep higher rates for critical ones, controlling cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail data events: not tracing.
• 100% sampling: raises cost.
• Disable tracing: loses visibility.

Key takeaway: control tracing cost → sampling rules.
Q001344:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail Insights detects unusual management API call volumes or error rates compared with a baseline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Event history: no anomaly detection.
• Config timeline: configuration.
• Integrity validation: tamper detection.

Key takeaway: unusual API activity → CloudTrail Insights.
Q001345:
Why this is correct:
Kinesis processes records continuously as they arrive, enabling sub-second rolling aggregates. Logs Insights queries stored logs on demand.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights triggers scaling: false.
• Can't query numbers: it can.
• Kinesis cheaper for any query: not the point.

Key takeaway: continuous computation → streaming.
Q001346:
Why this is correct:
Trails log management events by default. S3 object reads are data events and must be enabled to see who read the object.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 24-hour default: event history keeps 90 days.
• Never records S3: data events do.
• Versioning: unrelated.

Key takeaway: object-level auditing → S3 data events.
Q001347:
Why this is correct:
Sending S3 events to EventBridge lets rules route new-object events for the prefix to multiple targets without overlapping notification conflicts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Another notification: overlapping filters conflict.
• Config: not an event trigger.
• Polling: delayed.

Key takeaway: S3 events to many targets → EventBridge.
Q001348:
Why this is correct:
A composite alarm combines the three alarms' states into one notification, reducing noise.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Anomaly detection on all: still three alarms.
• SNS deduplication: not supported that way.
• One metric filter: metrics aren't logs.

Key takeaway: reduce alert noise → composite alarms.
Q001350:
Why this is correct:
On-demand absorbs sudden spikes immediately (up to double previous peaks, with limits), while auto scaling reacts over minutes and can throttle during sharp spikes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-demand always cheaper: not for steady load.
• Auto scaling reacts faster: it's slower.
• On-demand uses alarms: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: spiky DynamoDB → on-demand.
Q001351:
Why this is correct:
If the service is already at the scalable target's maximum capacity, target tracking can't add tasks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs subscription required: no.
• Fargate can't use target tracking: it can.
• Memory only: CPU works.

Key takeaway: check min/max bounds when scaling stalls.
Q001352:
Why this is correct:
The alarm publishes to SNS, which notifies on-call and invokes a Lambda function that runs the cleanup on the instance through SSM Run Command.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nightly reboot: not targeted.
• Metric filter to run scripts: not how it works.
• Config remediation from an alarm: not the mechanism here.

Key takeaway: alarm → SNS → Lambda → SSM for automated fixes.
Q001353:
Why this is correct:
A Config remediation action running an SSM Automation document installs and starts the CloudWatch agent on noncompliant instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inventory: reports, doesn't install.
• Email: manual.
• Config installs software: via SSM remediation, not directly.

Key takeaway: auto-fix instance configuration → Config + SSM Automation.
Q001354:
Why this is correct:
Brief slowness shouldn't fail targets. Raising the unhealthy threshold and/or the interval and timeout tolerates transient spikes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove health checks: unsafe.
• TCP checks: less meaningful.
• Shorter interval: more flapping.

Key takeaway: tune health checks to avoid flapping.
Q001355:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge Scheduler is built for large numbers of schedules, with time zones, one-time schedules, and flexible windows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config scheduled rules: compliance.
• Inspector scans: vulnerabilities.
• Logs scheduled queries: not a scheduler for Lambda.

Key takeaway: many schedules → EventBridge Scheduler.
Q001356:
Why this is correct:
Automatic termination can destroy production if the rule misfires. Manual approval adds a safety check at the cost of slower response.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Instance already terminated: false.
• No manual approval support: manual remediation exists.
• No EBS remediation: not the point.

Key takeaway: weigh blast radius before auto-remediating destructively.
Q001357:
Why this is correct:
Health organizational view aggregates events across accounts, and an EventBridge rule on aws.health events routes them to the security team.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rules in each account: more setup (though possible).
• Config aggregator: doesn't collect Health events.
• Email per account: fragmented.

Key takeaway: org-wide Health events → organizational view + EventBridge.
Q001358:
Why this is correct:
S3 object-level API calls (such as DeleteObject) are CloudTrail data events, not logged by default. Enable S3 data events so EventBridge receives them (or use S3 Event Notifications to EventBridge).

Why the other options are wrong:
• s3:GetObject permission: unrelated to triggering.
• CloudTrail doesn't deliver to EventBridge: it does.
• EventBridge can't match S3 calls: it can with data events.

Key takeaway: object-level events need data event logging.
Q001359:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule matching CreateAccessKey gives near-real-time alerts, and CloudTrail Insights detects anomalous call volumes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Periodic Config rules: slow.
• One metric filter: no anomaly baseline.
• GuardDuty alone: different detections.

Key takeaway: specific API alerts → EventBridge; anomalies → Insights.
Q001360:
Why this is correct:
Targeting an SQS queue buffers bursts, and Lambda polls with controlled batch sizes and concurrency, so findings aren't dropped or overwhelm downstream.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Express workflow: still concurrency concerns.
• Huge reserved concurrency: may overload downstream.
• Zero retries: loses events.

Key takeaway: buffer bursts with a queue.
Q001361:
Why this is correct:
Kinesis Data Streams handles high sustained ingest, preserves order per partition key (device ID), and supports multiple consumers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EventBridge bus: not for sustained high-volume streams.
• SQS FIFO: throughput limits.
• SNS: no ordering or replay.

Key takeaway: high-volume ordered streams → Kinesis.
Q001362:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions with waitForTaskToken can isolate the instance automatically, then pause for a human decision before further actions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduler: not event-driven.
• Lambda sleep: 15-minute limit.
• SSM automatic only: no human gate as described.

Key takeaway: automation with human approval → task tokens.
Q001363:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge Pipes connects a source (such as SQS) to a target with optional filtering, enrichment, and transformation, without writing glue code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Archive and replay: event history.
• Schema Registry: schemas.
• Chained rules: can't read from SQS.

Key takeaway: point-to-point source → target with transform → Pipes.
Q001364:
Why this is correct:
Root console sign-in events have their own source and detail-type (aws.signin, 'AWS Console Sign In via CloudTrail') and are delivered in specific Regions (for example, us-east-1 for global sign-ins). A pattern that doesn't match these misses them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Org trails ignore members: they log members.
• Root activity not logged: it is.
• Management account can't have rules: it can.

Key takeaway: match event patterns to the exact source, type, and Region.
Q001365:
Why this is correct:
Lambda destinations for asynchronous invocations capture the full event plus the result (on success) or error details (on failure) and send them to targets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• try/catch to SNS: custom and incomplete.
• DLQ: failed events only, without results.
• X-Ray: traces, not payload storage.

Key takeaway: async outcomes → destinations.
Q001366:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account forwarding needs the member account's rule to target the correct central bus ARN, and the central bus policy must allow that account to PutEvents.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config enabled: unrelated.
• GuardDuty in central account: unrelated to forwarding.
• Admin IAM user: unrelated.

Key takeaway: cross-account events = correct target + bus policy.
Q001368:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge Scheduler invokes the Lambda function every 15 minutes with no extra infrastructure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSM runbook via alarm: indirect.
• Step Functions wait loop: pays for orchestration.
• Config periodic rule: minimum intervals and wrong purpose.

Key takeaway: simple recurring invocation → EventBridge Scheduler.
Q001370:
Why this is correct:
A launch lifecycle hook holds new instances in Pending:Wait while EventBridge triggers an SSM runbook to configure them, then completes the hook so they enter service ready.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config after InService: too late.
• Grace period: doesn't run configuration.
• Synchronous user data only: no controlled gate or retry.

Key takeaway: gate new instances until ready → launch lifecycle hooks.
Q001371:
Why this is correct:
Config's built-in remediation with SSM documents provides retries, rate limits, and an audit trail. A custom Lambda offers flexibility but you build those features yourself.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda always cheaper: not the point.
• Can't use SSM: it uses SSM documents.
• Lambda gives better audit: Config tracks remediation.

Key takeaway: prefer managed remediation unless logic is custom.
Q001372:
Why this is correct:
Warm pools keep pre-initialized instances ready, so scale-out skips the 15-minute warm-up.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer grace period: doesn't speed readiness.
• Long lifecycle hooks: still wait each time.
• Scheduled scale-out hours early: wasteful and misses surprises.

Key takeaway: long initialization → warm pools.
Q001374:
Why this is correct:
Automatic remediation fails if SSM can't assume the remediation role or the role lacks s3:PutEncryptionConfiguration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Requires clicking: automatic remediation doesn't.
• Different Region: Config rules are Regional but that's not the issue.
• S3 unsupported: S3 is supported.

Key takeaway: remediation needs a working role with permissions.
Q001375:
Why this is correct:
SSM Automation runbooks aren't bound by Lambda's 15-minute limit and include many built-in actions for long operations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda can't be triggered by Config: it can.
• SSM free vs. Lambda: not the key reason.
• Python only: SSM supports multiple step types.

Key takeaway: long remediation → Automation runbooks.
Q001376:
Why this is correct:
An instance refresh replaces running instances gradually with ones launched from the updated template, respecting minimum healthy percentage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Wait for natural replacement: may never happen.
• Update the template again: doesn't replace instances.
• Terminate all at once: downtime.

Key takeaway: roll out new AMIs → instance refresh.
Q001380:
Why this is correct:
If the alarm's evaluation window is longer than the deployment bake time, the deployment completes before the alarm can fire, so no rollback occurs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda-only rollback: ECS supports it.
• In-place vs. blue/green: not the cause.
• EC2 only: ECS supports alarms.

Key takeaway: alarm windows must fit within bake time.
Q001382:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch alarms can create OpsCenter OpsItems automatically, giving a centralized, trackable record of each breach.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS email: not tracked.
• CloudTrail Insights: API anomalies.
• Config items: configuration, not alarm events.

Key takeaway: trackable operational issues → OpsItems.
Q001383:
Why this is correct:
A Synthetics canary exercising the external checkout path from outside detects failures that internal health checks can't see.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More frequent internal checks: still internal.
• Internal metrics: miss external path issues.
• Container Insights: resource metrics.

Key takeaway: external user experience → canaries.
Q001384:
Why this is correct:
Tasks that pass container startup but fail the ALB check get replaced in a loop. Check the target group health check path and port, and that security groups allow the ALB to reach tasks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Max CPU/memory: not the cause.
• Container Insights: monitoring only.
• Platform version: unlikely.

Key takeaway: cycling tasks → health checks and SG paths.
Q001385:
Why this is correct:
Container Insights collects pod and container metrics and logs, including restarts, to diagnose CrashLoopBackOff.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.
• X-Ray: request traces.
• Config: configuration.

Key takeaway: container health → Container Insights.
Q001386:
Why this is correct:
ServiceLens (now part of CloudWatch Application Signals) combines X-Ray traces with CloudWatch metrics and logs in one view.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray alone: limited integration.
• Detective: security investigations.
• Config aggregator: configuration.

Key takeaway: traces + metrics + logs together → ServiceLens.
Q001387:
Why this is correct:
A Health event about hardware degradation explains the failures. Verify the impact and automate responses (for example, EventBridge rules on Health events) for next time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unrelated: it's the cause.
• Dispute retirements: not appropriate.
• No action: automate future handling.

Key takeaway: Health events explain infrastructure-driven failures.
Q001388:
Why this is correct:
Drift detection compares current resource configurations with the template and shows differing properties.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't detect: it can.
• Manual comparison: slow.
• Config alone: doesn't compare with the template.

Key takeaway: manual changes to stacks → drift detection.
Q001389:
Why this is correct:
Requiring a unique ExternalId in the trust policy prevents the confused deputy problem when third parties assume the role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Source IP: fragile.
• Permissions boundary: limits permissions, not who can assume.
• MFA: third-party automated assumption may not use MFA.

Key takeaway: third-party roles → ExternalId.
Q001390:
Why this is correct:
SCPs don't affect the management account. If the developer is in the management account, the deny doesn't apply.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Allow overrides SCP: false.
• SCPs only affect root: false.
• Wrong OU: possible, but the telling case is the management account.

Key takeaway: SCPs never restrict the management account.
Q001391:
Why this is correct:
Role sessions from AssumeRole without MFA don't carry aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent, so a Deny-unless-MFA policy blocks CI/CD roles. Use BoolIfExists or exclude those roles.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Roles can't use MFA conditions: they can.
• Need an explicit Allow: the Deny still applies.
• Must use IAM users: no.

Key takeaway: MFA conditions and role sessions need care.
Q001392:
Why this is correct:
IRSA (or EKS Pod Identity) gives each service account its own IAM role and temporary credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Static credentials in Secrets Manager: long-term keys.
• Keys in Kubernetes Secrets: long-term keys.
• Node role for all pods: not least privilege.

Key takeaway: per-pod IAM → IRSA / Pod Identity.
Q001393:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account secrets need a Secrets Manager resource policy granting Account B's role, and a KMS key policy allowing it to decrypt (plus B's identity policy).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Key policy only: secret policy needed too.
• Secret policy only: key access needed too.
• Copy the key: not possible.

Key takeaway: cross-account secret = secret policy + key policy.
Q001397:
Why this is correct:
Resource control policies (RCPs) set org-wide limits on who can access resources, such as blocking external principals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Tag policies: tags.
• Declarative policies: account settings.
• SCPs: limit principals, not resources.

Key takeaway: restrict external access to resources → RCPs.
Q001398:
Why this is correct:
WAF rate-based rules can aggregate on keys other than IP (for example, headers) to catch distributed L7 floods, and Shield Advanced adds L3/L4 protection and cost protection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shield Advanced alone: needs WAF for L7 rules.
• WAF alone: not L3/L4.
• Security groups: not DDoS mitigation.

Key takeaway: L7 floods → WAF; L3/L4 → Shield Advanced.
Q001400:
Why this is correct:
AWS Network Firewall in the inspection VPC with domain-list rules enforces domain filtering for all traffic routed through the Transit Gateway.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security groups: no domain rules.
• Flow Logs remediation: reactive.
• WAF on ALBs: inbound HTTP only.

Key takeaway: central egress domain filtering → Network Firewall.
Q001403:
Why this is correct:
CloudHSM provides FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated, single-tenant HSMs, and can back a KMS custom key store.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-C: key management shifts to you, not an HSM.
• Secrets Manager identical to CloudHSM: false.
• Standard KMS keys: not dedicated HSMs you control.

Key takeaway: dedicated validated HSMs → CloudHSM.
Q001404:
Why this is correct:
Session Manager provides shell access without inbound ports or SSH keys, with IAM control and logging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bastion with the same rules: still exposed.
• VPN for SSH: still keys and ports.
• Office IP restriction: still SSH and keys.

Key takeaway: remove SSH exposure → Session Manager.
Q001406:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2 scans EBS volumes when suspicious activity is detected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda Protection: Lambda network activity.
• S3 Protection: S3 access.
• RDS Protection: database logins.

Key takeaway: scan EC2 volumes for malware → Malware Protection for EC2.
Q001407:
Why this is correct:
Detective builds behavior graphs from logs and findings to investigate what the instance did and with whom.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: best practices.
• Config: configuration.
• Macie: sensitive data.

Key takeaway: investigate findings → Detective.
Q001408:
Why this is correct:
ALBs need a REGIONAL web ACL in the ALB's Region. Recreate the web ACL with REGIONAL scope and associate it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Move the ALB: not how scopes work.
• Scope doesn't matter: it does.
• Firewall Manager bridging: doesn't change scope rules.

Key takeaway: ALB → REGIONAL web ACL.
Q001409:
Why this is correct:
Keys with imported key material can't use automatic rotation, and multi-Region keys rotate from the primary. Rotation behavior differs by key type.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Asymmetric keys rotate the same: they don't support automatic rotation.
• Multi-Region never rotates: they do via the primary.
• Identical for all: not true.

Key takeaway: rotation depends on key type and origin.
Q001411:
Why this is correct:
A Config rule for S3 default encryption with SSM auto-remediation fixes buckets within minutes, across accounts if deployed org-wide.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Alarm emails: manual.
• IAM deny on PutObject: blocks usage, doesn't fix.
• Weekly script: slow.

Key takeaway: auto-fix bucket settings → Config + remediation.
Q001412:
Why this is correct:
Flow log REJECT entries with permissive security groups point to the network ACL, which is stateless and may block traffic or return ports.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail: doesn't show traffic decisions.
• pkt-srcaddr: NAT visibility, not rejection cause.
• GuardDuty suppression: unrelated.

Key takeaway: REJECTs with open SGs → check NACLs.
Q001413:
Why this is correct:
Drift detection doesn't detect every change (for example, some properties or resources, and changes to list properties not in the template). Review supported resources and properties.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rollback state needed: no.
• SGs unsupported: they're supported, with property caveats.
• 24-hour automatic run: drift detection is on demand.

Key takeaway: drift detection has known gaps.
Q001415:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty detects anomalous behavior, such as credentials used from unusual locations. A Config rule detects configuration drift from standards.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Macie/GuardDuty swapped: incorrect.
• GuardDuty for both: doesn't do configuration compliance.
• Config for both: doesn't detect behavior.

Key takeaway: behavior → GuardDuty; configuration → Config.
Q001416:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail Insights detects unusual spikes in management API call volume, such as a 20× jump in RunInstances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Integrity validation: tampering.
• S3 data events: object calls.
• Config timeline: configuration.

Key takeaway: API volume anomalies → CloudTrail Insights.
Q001417:
Why this is correct:
GetObject calls are data events and must be enabled on the trail to be logged.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Never logs S3: data events do.
• Only Flow Logs: incorrect.
• Versioning needed: no.

Key takeaway: object access auditing → data events.
Q001418:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account subscription filters stream member accounts' logs into a central Kinesis stream in near real time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily exports: not near real time.
• Flow Logs instead: different data.
• Weekly CLI copies: manual.

Key takeaway: central real-time logs → cross-account subscriptions.
Q002034:
Why this is correct:
LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes sends 10% for 5 minutes, and an alarm on the deployment group rolls back automatically if errors rise.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Linear without alarms: no rollback.
• AllAtOnce: no gradual exposure.
• Manual alias weights: no automatic rollback.

Key takeaway: canary + alarms for safe Lambda releases.
Q002035:
Why this is correct:
The pipeline assumes a role in the production account (trusted by the tools account), and the artifact bucket's KMS key policy (and bucket policy) lets that role decrypt artifacts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Duplicate pipelines: drift.
• VPC peering: not needed.
• aws/s3 managed key: can't be shared cross-account.

Key takeaway: cross-account pipelines = assumed role + KMS/bucket access.
Q002036:
Why this is correct:
CodeArtifact with an external connection to npmjs caches packages centrally and lets security control what's used.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ECR OCI artifacts: not an npm registry.
• Manual S3 uploads: toil.
• Local CodeBuild cache: per project, no governance.

Key takeaway: central package caching → CodeArtifact.
Q002037:
Why this is correct:
Caching the Maven local repository (for example, ~/.m2) between builds avoids re-downloading dependencies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger EBS: not the bottleneck.
• Bigger compute: download time remains.
• Parallel pipelines: doesn't reduce downloads.

Key takeaway: repeated dependency downloads → build cache.
Q002038:
Why this is correct:
A service-managed StackSet targeting the OU with automatic deployment covers existing and future accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-managed with manual IDs: toil.
• Daily Lambda: reinvents StackSets.
• Account owners deploy: inconsistent.

Key takeaway: OU-wide baselines → service-managed StackSets.
Q002039:
Why this is correct:
UpdateReplacePolicy and DeletionPolicy set to Snapshot or Retain protect data when a replacement happens, and reviewing a change set reveals the replacement before executing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Drift detection: doesn't protect data.
• DeletionPolicy only: doesn't cover replacement.
• Termination protection: prevents stack deletion, not replacement.

Key takeaway: replacement risk → UpdateReplacePolicy + change sets.
Q002040:
Why this is correct:
The cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check Config rule periodically checks stacks for drift and can notify.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Termination protection: unrelated.
• Stack policy: doesn't stop console changes.
• Manual CloudTrail search: slow.

Key takeaway: continuous drift monitoring → Config drift rule.
Q002041:
Why this is correct:
A spread strategy on attribute:ecs.availability-zone places tasks evenly across AZs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• distinctInstance: different instances, possibly same AZ.
• binpack: concentrates tasks.
• Random with more tasks: no guarantee.

Key takeaway: AZ balance for ECS on EC2 → spread by AZ.
Q002042:
Why this is correct:
A termination lifecycle hook pauses termination until the application finishes and uploads, then completes the hook.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OldestInstance policy: chooses which, not how.
• Scale-in protection: blocks termination entirely.
• Deregistration delay: only connection draining.

Key takeaway: graceful scale-in → termination lifecycle hooks.
Q002043:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch cross-account observability links source accounts to a monitoring account for unified metrics, logs, and traces.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nightly S3 + Athena: not live.
• Kinesis per log group: logs only.
• IAM users everywhere: not a unified view.

Key takeaway: multi-account observability → cross-account observability.
Q002044:
Why this is correct:
EMF writes metrics in structured logs, extracted asynchronously by CloudWatch, avoiding PutMetricData throttling and latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More memory: still API limits.
• X-Ray annotations: not metrics.
• DynamoDB hourly: not real-time metrics.

Key takeaway: high-volume custom metrics → EMF.
Q002045:
Why this is correct:
A composite alarm pages only when the key symptoms (latency AND errors) are alarming, while other alarms can notify quietly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete alarms: loses signals.
• CPU anomaly only: misses symptoms.
• More periods: delays without deduplicating.

Key takeaway: alert on symptoms with composite alarms.
Q002046:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on the EC2 state-change (stopped) event starts an SSM Automation runbook that collects diagnostics and acts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ASG desired 0: unrelated.
• Dashboard review: manual.
• Hourly polling: slow.

Key takeaway: event-driven diagnostics → EventBridge + SSM.
Q002047:
Why this is correct:
When the previous revision's ApplicationStop script is broken, redeploy with the option to ignore ApplicationStop failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer timeout in the new appspec: the old script runs.
• Recreate the group: unnecessary.
• AllAtOnce: still runs the failing hook.

Key takeaway: broken old stop scripts → ignore ApplicationStop failures.
Q002048:
Why this is correct:
The restricted-ssh Config rule deployed org-wide with SSM auto-remediation fixes open SSH within minutes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCP denying all ingress changes: blocks legitimate use.
• Weekly Inspector review: slow.
• Trusted Advisor email: manual.

Key takeaway: auto-fix open SSH → Config + remediation.
Q002049:
Why this is correct:
A GuardDuty delegated administrator in each Region with auto-enable covers all current and future accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail Lake: not threat detection.
• Management account only: no coverage.
• Manual enable: toil.

Key takeaway: org-wide GuardDuty per Region → delegated admin + auto-enable.
Q002050:
Why this is correct:
Storing the token in Secrets Manager and referencing it in the buildspec env secrets-manager section keeps it out of code and logs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• README: exposed.
• Base64: not encryption.
• Plaintext console variable: exposed.

Key takeaway: build secrets → Secrets Manager references.
Q002051:
Why this is correct:
IAM Access Analyzer's unused access analyzer finds unused roles, access keys, passwords, and permissions across the organization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config inventory: no usage data.
• External access analyzer: public/cross-account access.
• Credential report: one account and limited.

Key takeaway: find unused access → unused access analyzer.
Q002052:
Why this is correct:
Allowing iam:CreateRole only when a specific permissions boundary is attached lets developers create roles that can't exceed the boundary.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared admin role: over-privileged.
• Deny CreateRole: blocks self-service.
• iam:* with monthly review: risky.

Key takeaway: safe delegated role creation → permissions boundaries.
